questions.text: What is the primary treatment goal in managing sinus tachycardia?
options: Identify and treat the underlying cause
originalOptions: Identify and treat the underlying cause
questions.correctAnswer: C) Identify and treat the underlying cause
questions.correctAnswerText: Identify and treat the underlying cause
questions.explanation: Sinus tachycardia is usually a physiologic response to an underlying stressor (pain, fever, hypovolemia, etc.); treating the cause resolves the tachycardia,whereas adenosine and cardioversion are for reentrant arrhythmias, not sinus tach.

questions.text: After delivering a defibrillation shock to a patient in VF/pulseless VT, what is the immediate next step?
options: Resume CPR immediately, starting with chest compressions
originalOptions: Resume CPR immediately, starting with chest compressions
questions.correctAnswer: A) Resume CPR immediately, starting with chest compressions
questions.correctAnswerText: Resume CPR immediately, starting with chest compressions
questions.explanation: CPR must resume immediately after a shock without pausing to check pulse or rhythm, since even a successful shock rarely produces an immediately palpable pulse; rhythm is reassessed after the 2-minute CPR cycle.

questions.text: In adult cardiac arrest, when is the first dose of epinephrine given, and how often is it repeated?
options: 1 mg IV/IO once, immediately after the first shock
1 mg IV/IO every 10 minutes throughout the arrest
2 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes starting immediately
1 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes, given as soon as possible in PEA/asystole or during the CPR cycle after the second shock in VF/pVT
originalOptions: 1 mg IV/IO once, immediately after the first shock
1 mg IV/IO every 10 minutes throughout the arrest
2 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes starting immediately
1 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes, given as soon as possible in PEA/asystole or during the CPR cycle after the second shock in VF/pVT
questions.correctAnswer: D) 1 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes, given as soon as possible in PEA/asystole or during the CPR cycle after the second shock in VF/pVT
questions.correctAnswerText: 1 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes, given as soon as possible in PEA/asystole or during the CPR cycle after the second shock in VF/pVT
questions.explanation: Epinephrine dosing is time-interval based (every 3-5 minutes), not a fixed number of doses, and its first administration differs by rhythm: immediate in PEA/asystole, after the second shock in VF/pVT.

questions.text: Which drug is used specifically to treat torsades de pointes during cardiac arrest management?
questions.correctAnswer: B) Magnesium sulfate
questions.explanation: Magnesium sulfate directly stabilizes the myocardial membrane in torsades de pointes, unlike amiodarone/lidocaine which are used for refractory VF/pVT, or sodium bicarbonate which is reserved for hyperkalemia, TCA overdose, or severe acidosis.

questions.text: Which of the following is used for cardiac reperfusion in an ACS patient when timely PCI is unavailable?
options: Fibrinolytic therapy, if the patient has an eligible STEMI and PCI is not available in time
originalOptions: Fibrinolytic therapy, if the patient has an eligible STEMI and PCI is not available in time
questions.correctAnswer: A) Fibrinolytic therapy, if the patient has an eligible STEMI and PCI is not available in time
questions.correctAnswerText: Fibrinolytic therapy, if the patient has an eligible STEMI and PCI is not available in time
questions.explanation: Fibrinolytics achieve coronary reperfusion when timely PCI cannot be performed; epinephrine and atropine have no role in coronary reperfusion.

questions.text: In the VF/pulseless VT algorithm, when are epinephrine and amiodarone typically administered relative to defibrillation?
options: Epinephrine after every shock; amiodarone after the first shock
Epinephrine every 10 minutes; amiodarone after the fifth shock
Epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, given during the CPR cycle after the second shock; amiodarone (or lidocaine) for refractory VF/pVT typically after the third shock
Epinephrine only once at the start; amiodarone continuously infused
originalOptions: Epinephrine after every shock; amiodarone after the first shock
Epinephrine every 10 minutes; amiodarone after the fifth shock
Epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, given during the CPR cycle after the second shock; amiodarone (or lidocaine) for refractory VF/pVT typically after the third shock
Epinephrine only once at the start; amiodarone continuously infused

questions.correctAnswerText: Epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, given during the CPR cycle after the second shock; amiodarone (or lidocaine) for refractory VF/pVT typically after the third shock
questions.explanation: The standard sequence gives epinephrine after the second shock and repeats it every 3-5 minutes; amiodarone/lidocaine are added for shock-refractory VF/pVT after the third shock, without ever replacing CPR or defibrillation.

questions.text: A 55-year-old male has stroke symptoms, and CT shows multilobar infarction (more than one-third of the cerebral hemisphere). What therapy is contraindicated?
questions.correctAnswer: A) Thrombolytic therapy
questions.explanation: A large established infarct substantially increases the risk of hemorrhagic transformation with thrombolysis; current decisions also weigh time window, disabling deficit, and modern imaging criteria rather than this legacy size cutoff alone.

questions.text: A 79-year-old patient in supraventricular tachycardia has a blood pressure of 80/50 and complains of chest discomfort with near-syncope. What is the next appropriate step?
questions.correctAnswer: D) Synchronized cardioversion
questions.explanation: Hypotension and chest discomfort attributable to the tachyarrhythmia define instability, requiring immediate synchronized cardioversion; carotid massage risks complications in elderly patients, and amiodarone/lidocaine are not first-line for unstable SVT.

questions.text: _______ access is preferred in cardiac arrest due to easy access and no interruption in CPR.
questions.correctAnswer: B) Peripheral
questions.explanation: Peripheral IV access can be obtained without interrupting chest compressions and carries fewer complications than central lines, making it the preferred first-line route during arrest.

questions.text: All of the following are bradycardic rhythms except:
questions.correctAnswer: B) Atrial fibrillation
questions.explanation: Atrial fibrillation is typically associated with an irregular, often rapid ventricular response, not bradycardia, unlike the listed AV blocks which characteristically slow ventricular rate.

questions.text: Choose the correct sequence of electrical activity in the heart for normal sinus rhythm.
options: SA node, Purkinje fibers, AV node, Bundle of His
Purkinje fibers, Bundle of His, AV node, SA node
SA node, AV node, Bundle of His, Purkinje fibers
AV node, SA node, Bundle of His, Purkinje fibers
originalOptions: SA node, Purkinje fibers, AV node, Bundle of His
Purkinje fibers, Bundle of His, AV node, SA node
SA node, AV node, Bundle of His, Purkinje fibers
AV node, SA node, Bundle of His, Purkinje fibers
questions.correctAnswer: C) SA node, AV node, Bundle of His, Purkinje fibers
questions.correctAnswerText: SA node, AV node, Bundle of His, Purkinje fibers
questions.explanation: The normal conduction pathway originates in the SA node, passes through the AV node, then the Bundle of His, and finally the Purkinje fibers to depolarize the ventricles.

questions.text: In children and infants, when should 2 minutes of CPR be given before activating EMS in a single-rescuer scenario?
options: Unresponsive victim with pulse and breathing
originalOptions: Unresponsive victim with pulse and breathing
questions.correctAnswer: A) Unwitnessed collapse
questions.explanation: For an unwitnessed pediatric collapse, a lone rescuer should perform about 2 minutes of CPR before leaving to activate EMS/get an AED, since the initial cause is often respiratory rather than a witnessed cardiac event.

questions.text: In CPR, what is the maximum time a rescuer should take to check for a pulse?
questions.correctAnswer: A) No more than 10 seconds
questions.explanation: If a definite pulse is not felt within 10 seconds, the rescuer should begin or resume CPR without further delay to avoid prolonging a no-flow state.

questions.text: Most cases of pediatric cardiac arrest begin with which underlying process?
questions.correctAnswer: B) Respiratory distress/failure or shock (asphyxial arrest)
questions.explanation: Unlike adults, most pediatric arrests are asphyxial, progressing from respiratory failure or shock rather than a primary shockable arrhythmia — this is why early ventilation is emphasized in pediatric resuscitation.

questions.text: What best describes the traditional stroke-care time benchmarks of ED evaluation within 10 minutes, neurologic evaluation within 25 minutes, and head CT read within 45 minutes of arrival?
options: These are current mandatory legal requirements in all hospitals
These are outdated absolute rules that should never be exceeded
These are legacy process targets; current care still requires immediate evaluation and rapid imaging without avoidable delay, per local stroke protocol
These times apply only to hemorrhagic stroke
originalOptions: These are current mandatory legal requirements in all hospitals
These are outdated absolute rules that should never be exceeded
These are legacy process targets; current care still requires immediate evaluation and rapid imaging without avoidable delay, per local stroke protocol
These times apply only to hemorrhagic stroke
questions.correctAnswer: C) These are legacy process targets; current care still requires immediate evaluation and rapid imaging without avoidable delay, per local stroke protocol
questions.correctAnswerText: These are legacy process targets; current care still requires immediate evaluation and rapid imaging without avoidable delay, per local stroke protocol
questions.explanation: These specific minute-benchmarks are legacy process targets rather than fixed universal rules; the underlying principle of minimizing delay to imaging and treatment remains current.

questions.text: When should out-of-hospital resuscitation efforts be terminated in adults?
options: After exactly 20 minutes of CPR regardless of rhythm
Based on a validated termination-of-resuscitation rule (arrest not witnessed by EMS, no shock delivered, no ROSC), combined with clinical judgment
originalOptions: After exactly 20 minutes of CPR regardless of rhythm
Based on a validated termination-of-resuscitation rule (arrest not witnessed by EMS, no shock delivered, no ROSC), combined with clinical judgment
questions.correctAnswer: C) Based on a validated termination-of-resuscitation rule (arrest not witnessed by EMS, no shock delivered, no ROSC), combined with clinical judgment
questions.correctAnswerText: Based on a validated termination-of-resuscitation rule (arrest not witnessed by EMS, no shock delivered, no ROSC), combined with clinical judgment
questions.explanation: Termination decisions rely on validated criteria and clinical/legal judgment rather than an arbitrary elapsed time; in-hospital decisions remain individualized.

questions.text: Select the proper pairing regarding chest compressions for an adult.
options: 100 to 120 compressions/minute; 2 to 2.4 inches (5-6 cm) deep
originalOptions: 100 to 120 compressions/minute; 2 to 2.4 inches (5-6 cm) deep
questions.correctAnswer: A) 100 to 120 compressions/minute; 2 to 2.4 inches (5-6 cm) deep
questions.correctAnswerText: 100 to 120 compressions/minute; 2 to 2.4 inches (5-6 cm) deep
questions.explanation: High-quality adult CPR requires a compression rate of 100-120/min and a depth of 5-6 cm, avoiding both underventilation of blood flow and excessive depth that risks injury.

questions.text: Symptomatic bradycardia (HR 32, hypotension, altered mental status): what is the first-line medication?
questions.correctAnswer: D) Atropine
questions.explanation: Atropine is the first-line drug for symptomatic bradycardia; dopamine or epinephrine infusions and transcutaneous pacing are reserved as next-line options if atropine fails, not co-first-line agents.

questions.text: In the treatment of a stable tachyarrhythmia, how many CPR cycles must elapse before reassessing the rhythm?
options: CPR cycles are not the relevant measure — reassessment depends on the patient's response to treatment (vagal maneuvers, adenosine, or cardioversion), not a fixed number of CPR cycles
originalOptions: CPR cycles are not the relevant measure — reassessment depends on the patient's response to treatment (vagal maneuvers, adenosine, or cardioversion), not a fixed number of CPR cycles
questions.correctAnswer: B) CPR cycles are not the relevant measure — reassessment depends on the patient's response to treatment (vagal maneuvers, adenosine, or cardioversion), not a fixed number of CPR cycles
questions.correctAnswerText: CPR cycles are not the relevant measure — reassessment depends on the patient's response to treatment (vagal maneuvers, adenosine, or cardioversion), not a fixed number of CPR cycles
questions.explanation: The tachycardia-with-a-pulse algorithm is response-driven, not cycle-counted like the pulseless arrest algorithm; "5 CPR cycles" is a pulseless-arrest concept misapplied here.

questions.text: The 6 steps in the Adult Chain of Survival include all of the following except:
questions.correctAnswer: D) Use of cardiovascular medications
questions.explanation: The Chain of Survival emphasizes early recognition/CPR, rapid defibrillation, and integrated post-arrest care; routine cardiovascular medications are not one of its defined links.
questions.note: The Adult Chain of Survival (AHA, out-of-hospital version) has 6 links: 1. Recognition of cardiac arrest and activation of emergency response . 2. Early, high-quality CPR . 3. Rapid defibrillation . 4. Advanced resuscitation (ACLS) . 5. Post-cardiac arrest care . 6. Recovery .

questions.text: Which elements are included in the ACLS Survey?
questions.correctAnswer: C) Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Differential diagnosis
questions.explanation: The ACLS Survey (as opposed to the BLS Survey) systematically assesses Airway, Breathing, Circulation, and Differential diagnosis to identify and treat reversible causes.

questions.text: What term describes an organized electrical rhythm with no palpable pulse, and how is it treated?
options: Pulseless electrical activity (PEA); treat with high-quality CPR, epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, and correction of reversible causes (do not shock)
Ventricular fibrillation; treat with immediate defibrillation
Pulseless VT; treat with synchronized cardioversion
originalOptions: Pulseless electrical activity (PEA); treat with high-quality CPR, epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, and correction of reversible causes (do not shock)
Ventricular fibrillation; treat with immediate defibrillation
Pulseless VT; treat with synchronized cardioversion
questions.correctAnswer: A) Pulseless electrical activity (PEA); treat with high-quality CPR, epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, and correction of reversible causes (do not shock)
questions.correctAnswerText: Pulseless electrical activity (PEA); treat with high-quality CPR, epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, and correction of reversible causes (do not shock)
questions.explanation: PEA is defined by an organized rhythm without a detectable pulse; it is not shockable, so treatment centers on CPR, epinephrine, and correcting the underlying Hs and Ts

questions.text: The normal sinus rhythm of the heart starts in the:
questions.correctAnswer: D) Sinoatrial node
questions.explanation: The SA node is the heart's natural pacemaker, initiating the electrical impulse that spreads through the atria to the AV node.

questions.text: The primary focus of treating cardiac arrest is:
options: Both effective CPR and early defibrillation
originalOptions: Both effective CPR and early defibrillation
questions.correctAnswer: B) Both effective CPR and early defibrillation
questions.correctAnswerText: Both effective CPR and early defibrillation
questions.explanation: High-quality CPR and early defibrillation are the two interventions most strongly linked to survival in cardiac arrest, more so than drug administration.

questions.text: A 3-year-old child begins breathing at 18 breaths/min and has a pulse of 50/min. What should you do next?
questions.correctAnswer: A) Begin CPR with chest compressions
questions.explanation: CPR should be initiated in pediatric patients whose pulse is ≤60/min despite adequate oxygenation and ventilation, since this reflects inadequate perfusion.

questions.text: What age is considered an infant for BLS purposes?
questions.correctAnswer: C) Under one year
questions.explanation: BLS classifications define an infant as under one year of age, a child as 1 year to puberty, and adolescents and older as the adult category.

questions.text: What does the QRS complex on an ECG represent?
questions.correctAnswer: A) Ventricular contraction
questions.explanation: The QRS complex reflects ventricular depolarization leading to contraction; the T wave, not the QRS, represents ventricular repolarization.

questions.text: What factor is critical to assess in any emergency situation before approaching the patient?
questions.correctAnswer: D) Scene safety
questions.explanation: Scene safety must always be confirmed first so the rescuer does not become a second casualty, before any patient-specific assessment is made.

questions.text: What is the first step in the assessment of an individual found "down"?
options: Check to see if they are conscious or unconscious
originalOptions: Check to see if they are conscious or unconscious
questions.correctAnswer: B) Check to see if they are conscious or unconscious
questions.correctAnswerText: Check to see if they are conscious or unconscious
questions.explanation: Establishing responsiveness is the first assessment step, as it determines whether the emergency response/resuscitation sequence should be activated.

questions.text: What is the recommended method to monitor breathing/ventilation during ACLS care?
questions.correctAnswer: B) Capnography

questions.text: Where should you attempt to perform a pulse check in an adult?
questions.correctAnswer: C) Carotid artery
questions.explanation: The carotid artery is the standard site for adult pulse checks due to its accessibility and reliability during low-flow states.

questions.text: Which of the following is first-line treatment for ACS?
questions.correctAnswer: C) Aspirin, unless contraindicated
questions.explanation: Aspirin provides mortality benefit in acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and is given to essentially all eligible patients, whereas morphine and nitroglycerin are selective symptom therapies rather than universal first-line treatment.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT an example of an advanced airway?
questions.correctAnswer: A) Oropharyngeal airway
questions.explanation: An OPA is a basic airway adjunct, unlike the esophageal-tracheal tube, laryngeal mask airway, and Combitube, which are all advanced airway devices.

questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding BLS?
options: It has little impact on survival
It should be mastered prior to ACLS
originalOptions: It has little impact on survival
It should be mastered prior to ACLS
questions.correctAnswer: D) It should be mastered prior to ACLS
questions.correctAnswerText: It should be mastered prior to ACLS
questions.explanation: ACLS providers are presumed to have already mastered BLS skills, since high-quality CPR remains foundational to resuscitation outcomes.

questions.text: Which sequence best represents the adult Chain of Survival?
options: Check responsiveness, call EMS/AED, provide ventilations, defibrillate, recovery
Check responsiveness, call EMS/AED, begin chest compressions, provide early defibrillation, recovery
Check responsiveness, call EMS/AED, defibrillate, recovery
Check responsiveness, call EMS/AED, wait for advanced care, recovery
originalOptions: Check responsiveness, call EMS/AED, provide ventilations, defibrillate, recovery
Check responsiveness, call EMS/AED, begin chest compressions, provide early defibrillation, recovery
Check responsiveness, call EMS/AED, defibrillate, recovery
Check responsiveness, call EMS/AED, wait for advanced care, recovery
questions.correctAnswer: B) Check responsiveness, call EMS/AED, begin chest compressions, provide early defibrillation, recovery
questions.correctAnswerText: Check responsiveness, call EMS/AED, begin chest compressions, provide early defibrillation, recovery
questions.explanation: The Chain of Survival emphasizes early CPR (chest compressions) and early defibrillation as the key steps between activation of emergency response and recovery.

questions.text: While one rescuer is performing CPR on an infant, a second rescuer arrives. What should happen next?
options: The second rescuer takes over compressions alone while the first rescuer leaves
The second rescuer waits until the first rescuer is exhausted
The second rescuer immediately applies AED pads without confirming EMS activation
The second rescuer activates the emergency response system/retrieves the AED if not already done, then assists with two-rescuer CPR
originalOptions: The second rescuer takes over compressions alone while the first rescuer leaves
The second rescuer waits until the first rescuer is exhausted
The second rescuer immediately applies AED pads without confirming EMS activation
The second rescuer activates the emergency response system/retrieves the AED if not already done, then assists with two-rescuer CPR
questions.correctAnswer: D) The second rescuer activates the emergency response system/retrieves the AED if not already done, then assists with two-rescuer CPR
questions.correctAnswerText: The second rescuer activates the emergency response system/retrieves the AED if not already done, then assists with two-rescuer CPR
questions.explanation: Two-rescuer infant CPR uses coordinated roles — one ensures EMS/AED activation while the other continues compressions — rather than one rescuer working alone or waiting

questions.text: During adult CPR with an advanced airway in place, what ventilation rate should be used?
options: One breath every 6 seconds with continuous chest compressions
originalOptions: One breath every 6 seconds with continuous chest compressions
questions.correctAnswer: C) One breath every 6 seconds with continuous chest compressions
questions.correctAnswerText: One breath every 6 seconds with continuous chest compressions
questions.explanation: Once an advanced airway is placed, compressions are continuous and ventilations are delivered asynchronously at one breath every 6 seconds (10/min), avoiding pauses in compressions.

questions.text: You are alone with an unresponsive 3-year-old child who is not breathing and appears cyanotic. What should you do first?
options: Give about 2 minutes of CPR, then activate EMS and get an AED
Leave immediately to activate EMS and get an AED
Give rescue breaths only for 2 minutes
Place the child in the recovery position
originalOptions: Give about 2 minutes of CPR, then activate EMS and get an AED
Leave immediately to activate EMS and get an AED
Give rescue breaths only for 2 minutes
Place the child in the recovery position
questions.correctAnswer: A) Give about 2 minutes of CPR, then activate EMS and get an AED
questions.correctAnswerText: Give about 2 minutes of CPR, then activate EMS and get an AED
questions.explanation: For an unwitnessed pediatric arrest with a lone rescuer, 2 minutes of CPR should be performed before leaving the child to activate EMS/retrieve an AED, since pediatric arrests are often asphyxial and respond to early ventilation/compressions.

questions.text: You are transporting an individual who goes into cardiac arrest during transport. IV access is unsuccessful. What is the next step?
options: Administer all medications through the ET tube
originalOptions: Administer all medications through the ET tube
questions.correctAnswer: D) Obtain intraosseous access
questions.explanation: IO access can be established rapidly and is the preferred next route for drug delivery when IV access fails, since ET tube drug absorption is unreliable and central lines interrupt CPR.

questions.text: CPR is initiated and the patient's pulse returns, but he is not breathing normally. What ventilation rate should be used?
options: 10 breaths per minute (1 breath every 6 seconds), with visible chest rise
originalOptions: 10 breaths per minute (1 breath every 6 seconds), with visible chest rise
questions.correctAnswer: B) 10 breaths per minute (1 breath every 6 seconds), with visible chest rise
questions.correctAnswerText: 10 breaths per minute (1 breath every 6 seconds), with visible chest rise
questions.explanation: For an adult with a pulse who is not breathing normally, rescue breathing is given at one breath every 6 seconds (10/min) with visible chest rise, per current AHA guidance.

questions.text: What is the single-rescuer adult chest compression-to-ventilation ratio before placement of an advanced airway?
options: 30 compressions to 2 breaths, before placement of an advanced airway
originalOptions: 30 compressions to 2 breaths, before placement of an advanced airway
questions.correctAnswer: C) 30 compressions to 2 breaths, before placement of an advanced airway
questions.correctAnswerText: 30 compressions to 2 breaths, before placement of an advanced airway

A) Continuous compressions at 100-120/min with 1 breath every 6 seconds B) 30:2 C) 15:2 D) 30:1 Correct Answer: A) Continuous compressions at 100-120/min with 1 breath every 6 seconds Explanation: After advanced airway placement, compressions become continuous (not paused for breaths) while ventilations are delivered asynchronously every 6 seconds.

questions.text: During high-quality CPR, what ETCO2 range indicates adequate chest compressions?
questions.correctAnswer: D) 10-20 mmHg
questions.explanation: An ETCO2 of at least 10-20 mmHg during CPR reflects adequate compressions and perfusion; persistently low ETCO2 suggests poor CPR quality, while a sudden rise to ≥40 mmHg suggests ROSC.

questions.text: According to current guidelines, what is the pediatric chest compression-to-ventilation ratio for single-rescuer versus two-rescuer CPR (without an advanced airway)?
options: 15:2 for all scenarios regardless of rescuer number
30:2 for all scenarios regardless of rescuer number
originalOptions: 15:2 for all scenarios regardless of rescuer number
30:2 for all scenarios regardless of rescuer number
questions.correctAnswer: B) 30:2 for single-rescuer; 15:2 for two-rescuer
questions.explanation: Pediatric CPR uses 30:2 for a lone rescuer (matching adult ratio) but shifts to 15:2 when a second rescuer is present to allow more frequent ventilation for the child.

questions.text: What are the possible effects of hyperventilation during CPR?
options: Increased intrathoracic pressure and decreased venous return to the heart (both)
Decreased venous return to the heart
originalOptions: Increased intrathoracic pressure and decreased venous return to the heart (both)
Decreased venous return to the heart
questions.correctAnswer: B) Increased intrathoracic pressure and decreased venous return to the heart (both)
questions.correctAnswerText: Increased intrathoracic pressure and decreased venous return to the heart (both)
questions.explanation: Excessive ventilation raises intrathoracic pressure, which impedes venous return to the heart and reduces cardiac output generated by compressions.

questions.text: Why are ventilations given to a pediatric arrest victim before seeking assistance in a single-rescuer scenario?
options: Most pediatric cardiac arrests are due to respiratory arrest
AED use is contraindicated in pediatrics
originalOptions: Most pediatric cardiac arrests are due to respiratory arrest
AED use is contraindicated in pediatrics
questions.correctAnswer: C) Most pediatric cardiac arrests are due to respiratory arrest
questions.correctAnswerText: Most pediatric cardiac arrests are due to respiratory arrest
questions.explanation: Since pediatric arrests are predominantly asphyxial, restoring oxygenation/ventilation early can be lifesaving and may prevent progression to full cardiac arrest

questions.text: Pulseless electrical activity (PEA) includes any pulseless rhythm EXCEPT which of the following?
options: Ventricular fibrillation, pulseless VT, and true asystole
originalOptions: Ventricular fibrillation, pulseless VT, and true asystole
questions.correctAnswer: D) Ventricular fibrillation, pulseless VT, and true asystole
questions.correctAnswerText: Ventricular fibrillation, pulseless VT, and true asystole
questions.explanation: PEA is defined as any organized pulseless rhythm; VF, pulseless VT, and true asystole are managed as separate distinct categories in the cardiac arrest algorithm and are excluded from the PEA definition.

questions.text: Which of the following can present as pulseless electrical activity (PEA)?
options: Any organized rhythm without a pulse (e.g., sinus rhythm, sinus bradycardia, idioventricular, or junctional rhythm)
originalOptions: Any organized rhythm without a pulse (e.g., sinus rhythm, sinus bradycardia, idioventricular, or junctional rhythm)
questions.correctAnswer: B) Any organized rhythm without a pulse (e.g., sinus rhythm, sinus bradycardia, idioventricular, or junctional rhythm)
questions.correctAnswerText: Any organized rhythm without a pulse (e.g., sinus rhythm, sinus bradycardia, idioventricular, or junctional rhythm)
questions.explanation: PEA encompasses any organized electrical activity on the monitor that lacks a detectable pulse, while VF, pulseless VT, and asystole are treated as separate rhythm categories.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a cause of pulseless electrical activity (PEA)?
questions.correctAnswer: B) Hyperventilation
questions.explanation: PEA causes follow the 5H/5T mnemonic (Hypoxia, Hypovolemia, Hydrogen ion/acidosis, Hypo/Hyperkalemia, Hypothermia, Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thrombosis, Trauma); hyperventilation is not one of these reversible causes.

questions.text: Which medication can be used to treat hypotension during the post-cardiac arrest phase?
questions.correctAnswer: C) Dopamine
questions.explanation: Dopamine is a vasopressor/inotrope used to support blood pressure in the post-arrest period; amiodarone treats arrhythmias, and milrinone is not typically used for post-arrest hypotension.

questions.text: After activating EMS and sending someone for an AED, what is the correct action for one-rescuer BLS of an unresponsive individual with no pulse?
questions.correctAnswer: A) Begin chest compressions
questions.explanation: Once help has been activated, the lone rescuer should immediately begin chest compressions, since compressions take priority in adult CPR sequencing.

questions.text: In which of the following situations should the AED NOT be applied without first modifying the patient or environment?
options: Victim with an implanted pacemaker (pad placement adjusted)
Victim with a transdermal medication patch (patch removed first)
Victim lying partially in water (should be moved to a dry area first)
originalOptions: Victim with an implanted pacemaker (pad placement adjusted)
Victim with a transdermal medication patch (patch removed first)
Victim lying partially in water (should be moved to a dry area first)
questions.correctAnswer: D) Victim lying partially in water (should be moved to a dry area first)
questions.correctAnswerText: Victim lying partially in water (should be moved to a dry area first)
questions.explanation: Water on the chest can short-circuit or reduce shock delivery, so the victim must be moved to a dry area and dried before AED use; pacemakers and patches only require adjusted pad placement or removal, not avoidance of the AED.

questions.text: A patient with a pulse has unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with hypotension and altered mental status. What is the indicated treatment?
questions.correctAnswer: B) Synchronized cardioversion
questions.explanation: Unstable VT with a pulse requires immediate synchronized cardioversion; amiodarone is an adjunct for stable or refractory VT, not the first action in instability.

questions.text: At what age is it preferable to use pediatric AED pads instead of adult pads?
questions.correctAnswer: C) Less than 8 years of age
questions.explanation: Pediatric AED pads/attenuated energy settings are preferred for children under 8 years old to deliver an age-appropriate energy dose; adult pads are used for older children and adults.

questions.text: How much energy is delivered for an adult shock with a monophasic defibrillator?
questions.explanation: Monophasic defibrillators deliver a fixed 360 J for all adult shocks, unlike biphasic devices which use 120-200 J per manufacturer recommendation.

questions.text: A patient in pulseless VT receives CPR/defibrillation cycles and remains pulseless, now with an organized SVT-like rhythm on the monitor. What is the next step?
options: Treat as pulseless electrical activity (PEA): resume high-quality CPR, give epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, and treat reversible causes; do not shock unless VF/pulseless VT recurs
Continue treating as pulseless VT with another shock
Give adenosine to convert the SVT-like rhythm
Shock the new rhythm since it originated from pulseless VT

Continue treating as pulseless VT with another shock
Give adenosine to convert the SVT-like rhythm
Shock the new rhythm since it originated from pulseless VT

questions.correctAnswerText: A premature wide QRS complex, usually without a preceding normal P wave, ٪؜ followed by a compensatory pause
questions.explanation: PVCs arise from ventricular ectopic foci, producing an early, wide, bizarre QRS without a preceding P wave, and the post-ectopic pause creates the "skipped beat" sensation patients report.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a classic sign of appendicitis?
questions.correctAnswer: C) Grey Turner sign
questions.explanation: Grey Turner's sign (flank ecchymosis) reflects retroperitoneal hemorrhage, classically severe hemorrhagic pancreatitis, not appendicitis; RLQ tenderness, rebound, Rovsing, and psoas/obturator signs are appendicitis findings.

questions.text: The psoas sign is tested by passive extension of the right hip, often with the patient in the left lateral position. What does a positive result suggest?
options: Retrocecal appendicitis or psoas muscle irritation
originalOptions: Retrocecal appendicitis or psoas muscle irritation
questions.correctAnswer: A) Retrocecal appendicitis or psoas muscle irritation
questions.correctAnswerText: Retrocecal appendicitis or psoas muscle irritation
questions.explanation: Passive hip extension stretches the iliopsoas muscle, reproducing pain when an inflamed retrocecal appendix (or a retroperitoneal process) lies against it; it is supportive but neither sensitive nor specific enough to rule appendicitis in or out alone.

questions.text: What proportion of appendicitis patients present with the full classic combination of fever, nausea/vomiting, RLQ pain, and leukocytosis?
questions.correctAnswer: D) About 20%
questions.explanation: Only around 20% of patients show the complete classic tetrad; this is a general limitation of clinical diagnosis, not specific to elderly patients (who in fact tend to have even more atypical presentations).

questions.text: A patient has RUQ pain, localized tenderness, no fever, no peritonism, a negative Murphy sign, and ultrasound showing a gallstone with acoustic shadowing. After pain control, what is the best disposition?
options: Discharge with analgesia, return precautions, and elective surgical referral
originalOptions: Discharge with analgesia, return precautions, and elective surgical referral
questions.correctAnswer: B) Discharge with analgesia, return precautions, and elective surgical referral
questions.correctAnswerText: Discharge with analgesia, return precautions, and elective surgical referral
questions.explanation: This presentation is uncomplicated biliary colic (no fever, peritonism, or Murphy sign); once pain resolves and vitals/labs are reassuring, outpatient management with elective cholecystectomy referral is appropriate, reserving admission/urgent intervention for complicated disease.

questions.text: Which statement about choledocholithiasis is correct?
options: It requires a common bile duct dilated below 5-7 mm
It always presents with Charcot's triad
It is defined by the presence of a stone in the common bile duct, and the duct may be normal or dilated

questions.correctAnswerText: It is defined by the presence of a stone in the common bile duct, and the duct may be normal or dilated
questions.explanation: Choledocholithiasis is defined by stone location (CBD), not by a specific duct diameter cutoff; duct diameter thresholds are age- and context-dependent, and cholangitis is a distinct, more severe infectious complication.

questions.text: Murphy's sign — inspiratory arrest on deep palpation under the right costal margin — is characteristic of which condition?
questions.correctAnswer: C) Acute cholecystitis
questions.explanation: Murphy's sign reflects gallbladder inflammation causing pain-induced inspiratory arrest when the inflamed gallbladder contacts the examiner's fingers; it is not a feature of appendicitis, for which psoas/Rovsing signs are used instead.

questions.text: Which term describes infection of the biliary tree, usually occurring behind an obstructed common bile duct?
questions.correctAnswer: A) Cholangitis
questions.explanation: Cholangitis is biliary tree infection typically from CBD obstruction (often by a stone), presenting with Charcot's triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain), which can progress to Reynolds' pentad with hypotension and altered mental status; this differs from cholecystitis, which is gallbladder inflammation from cystic-duct obstruction.

questions.text: Which statement about Meckel's diverticulum is FALSE?
options: It is more common in females
originalOptions: It is more common in females
questions.correctAnswer: D) It is more common in females
questions.correctAnswerText: It is more common in females
questions.explanation: Meckel diverticulum complications are actually more common in males; ectopic gastric/pancreatic tissue, bleeding, and the "rule of 2s" (2 inches long, 2 feet from the ileocecal valve, ~2% of population) are classic true associations.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT considered an independent predictor of adverse outcome in upper GI bleeding?
questions.correctAnswer: B) Initial hematocrit <45%
questions.explanation: A hematocrit below 45% is not itself a validated adverse-outcome threshold; the recognized poor-prognostic features include hematocrit <30%, SBP <100 mmHg, red blood on NG lavage, and cirrhosis/ascites, since initial hematocrit can lag behind acute blood loss.

questions.text: What does visible blood in a nasogastric aspirate suggest in a patient with GI bleeding?
options: It excludes a lower-GI source definitively
A negative aspirate excludes an upper-GI bleed
It supports an upper-GI source and higher-risk bleeding, but a negative aspirate does not exclude an upper-GI bleed
It is diagnostic of Mallory-Weiss tear

A negative aspirate excludes an upper-GI bleed
It supports an upper-GI source and higher-risk bleeding, but a negative aspirate does not exclude an upper-GI bleed
It is diagnostic of Mallory-Weiss tear
questions.correctAnswer: D) It supports an upper-GI source and higher-risk bleeding, but a negative aspirate does not exclude an upper-GI bleed
questions.correctAnswerText: It supports an upper-GI source and higher-risk bleeding, but a negative aspirate does not exclude an upper-GI bleed
questions.explanation: A bloody NG aspirate raises suspicion for an upper-GI source and higher-risk bleeding, but a clear aspirate can occur even with active upper-GI bleeding (e.g., duodenal source with pylorospasm), so it cannot rule it out.

questions.text: A patient with chronic alcohol-related liver disease presents with hematemesis. Which source of upper-GI bleeding must be urgently considered?
questions.correctAnswer: C) Esophageal or gastric variceal hemorrhage
questions.explanation: Chronic liver disease predisposes to portal hypertension and variceal bleeding, which requires urgent vasoactive/antibiotic therapy and endoscopy; however, chronic alcohol use alone does not confirm the diagnosis, so other causes should still be considered.

questions.text: A patient presents with acute right lower quadrant pain and McBurney's point tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis and initial management approach?

Testicular torsion; urgent urology consult only
Nonspecific abdominal pain; discharge with follow-up

questions.explanation: McBurney's point tenderness in the RLQ is classic for acute appendicitis, prompting confirmatory imaging (modality chosen by age/pregnancy status), supportive care, and prompt surgical evaluation.

questions.text: Which statement about angiodysplasia is correct?

questions.explanation: Angiodysplasia represents acquired, fragile vascular ectasias prone to intermittent bleeding, most commonly in the cecum/right colon, unlike the false premise that these are healthy, non-bleeding vessels.

questions.text: Which set of features supports a diagnosis of nonspecific abdominal pain (NSAP) as a diagnosis of exclusion?
options: Peritonism, toxic appearance, and worsening symptoms

Positive imaging for a surgical cause

questions.correctAnswerText: Hemodynamic stability, no peritonism/toxic appearance, mild or nonlocalizing tenderness, normal/nondiagnostic investigations, and improving symptoms tolerating oral intake
questions.explanation: NSAP is a diagnosis of exclusion made after ruling out surgical emergencies; it is characterized by stability, absence of peritoneal signs, nondiagnostic workup, and clinical improvement, with reliable follow-up arranged.

questions.text: What does the cremasteric reflex assess, and what is its clinical significance?
options: Stroking the inner thigh causes ipsilateral testicular elevation via cremaster muscle contraction; it is commonly absent in testicular torsion
Stroking the lateral thigh causes contralateral testicular elevation; it confirms epididymitis

It has no clinical significance in scrotal pain evaluation

questions.text: How should a patient with an Alvarado score of 6 be managed?
options: Immediate discharge with no further workup
Oral antibiotics alone as outpatient therapy
originalOptions: Immediate discharge with no further workup
Oral antibiotics alone as outpatient therapy
questions.correctAnswer: C) Observation/admission with further imaging
questions.explanation: An intermediate (5,6 score) does not reliably confirm or exclude appendicitis, so further imaging and reassessment (rather than discharge or immediate surgery) is the appropriate next step.

questions.text: Among alcohol, gallstones, idiopathic disease, hypertriglyceridemia, and snake bite, which is the LEAST typical cause of acute pancreatitis?
questions.correctAnswer: A) Snake bite
questions.explanation: Gallstones and alcohol are the most common causes of pancreatitis, with hypertriglyceridemia and idiopathic disease also well-established; venom-related pancreatitis is rare and classically associated with scorpion (not snake) envenomation in teaching mnemonics.

questions.text: What is the most common overall cause of acute abdominal pain presenting to the emergency department?
questions.correctAnswer: C) Nonspecific abdominal pain
questions.explanation: Nonspecific abdominal pain accounts for the largest proportion (roughly a third) of ED abdominal pain presentations overall, though the most common surgical cause or the leading cause in a specific age group may differ.

questions.text: What is the most significant risk factor for developing an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA)?
questions.correctAnswer: B) Smoking
questions.explanation: Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for AAA; other risk factors include age >65, male sex, hypertension, COPD, family history, and atherosclerosis, whereas diabetes is paradoxically associated with a lower AAA risk.

questions.text: Is mild, nonlocalizing tenderness compatible with a diagnosis of nonspecific abdominal pain?
options: No, NSAP requires a completely painless abdomen

False, tenderness always indicates a surgical cause

questions.correctAnswerText: True; NSAP is a diagnosis of exclusion but can include mild, nonlocalizing tenderness
questions.explanation: NSAP can present with mild, nonlocalizing tenderness, but guarding, rigidity, rebound, hemodynamic instability, or a toxic appearance should prompt evaluation for a specific serious cause before the diagnosis of exclusion is made.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a major compartment for occult blood loss causing hemorrhagic shock in an adult?
questions.correctAnswer: C) Head (intracranial space)
questions.explanation: Intracranial hemorrhage is neurologically devastating but the closed, limited cranial vault cannot accommodate enough blood loss to cause systemic hemorrhagic shock in an adult, unlike the chest, abdomen/retroperitoneum, pelvis, and long bones.

questions.text: At what age does testicular torsion most commonly occur?
questions.correctAnswer: A) Adolescence, approximately 12-16 years
questions.explanation: Testicular torsion peaks during adolescence; while it can occur at any age (so older age doesn't exclude it), only a minority of cases occur after age 20.

questions.text: A patient presents with acute RUQ pain, no fever, and imaging revealing gallstones without other complicating features. What is the next step?
options: Analgesia with follow-up for elective cholecystectomy
originalOptions: Analgesia with follow-up for elective cholecystectomy
questions.correctAnswer: D) Analgesia with follow-up for elective cholecystectomy
questions.correctAnswerText: Analgesia with follow-up for elective cholecystectomy
questions.explanation: Afebrile biliary colic without inflammatory or obstructive features (no Murphy sign, jaundice, or duct dilation) is managed with analgesia and elective surgical follow-up, reserving admission and urgent intervention for complicated disease.

questions.text: Which statement about biliary colic pain is correct?
options: It is specifically triggered only by protein intake
It may radiate to the right shoulder or subscapular region

It is relieved specifically by antacids

questions.explanation: Biliary colic classically radiates to the right shoulder/subscapular area due to shared phrenic nerve innervation; episodes are commonly precipitated by fatty meals, but timing and triggers vary between patients.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a sign of retroperitoneal hemorrhage?
questions.correctAnswer: C) Battle sign
questions.explanation: Battle sign (mastoid ecchymosis) suggests a basilar skull fracture, not retroperitoneal bleeding; Cullen sign (periumbilical) and Grey Turner sign (flank) are both associated with intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal hemorrhage.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about testicular torsion is WRONG?

Spontaneous detorsion occurs in about 10% of cases
originalOptions: Rapid growth of the testis may predispose to torsion
Spontaneous detorsion occurs in about 10% of cases

questions.explanation: Testicular torsion actually peaks in adolescence (approximately 12-16 years), not the 20-30 age range; rapid testicular growth and spontaneous detorsion in a minority of cases are recognized features.

questions.text: Is serum lactate a sensitive marker to rule out acute bowel ischemia?

questions.text: Is the pain of acute mesenteric ischemia sometimes poorly relieved by analgesics?

questions.text: How does the classic symptom triad of chronic mesenteric ischemia differ from acute mesenteric ischemia?
options: Chronic disease causes sudden severe pain; acute disease causes postprandial pain and weight loss

questions.correctAnswerText: Chronic disease causes postprandial pain, food fear, and weight loss; acute disease causes sudden severe pain out of proportion to exam findings
questions.explanation: Chronic mesenteric ischemia reflects progressive atherosclerotic narrowing causing "intestinal angina" (postprandial pain, sitophobia, weight loss), whereas acute ischemia presents abruptly with severe pain disproportionate to initially unremarkable exam findings.

questions.text: What is the preferred initial imaging test when acute mesenteric ischemia is suspected?
questions.correctAnswer: D) Contrast-enhanced CT (CT angiography)
questions.explanation: CT angiography is the preferred rapid diagnostic study for suspected acute mesenteric ischemia, allowing prompt visualization of mesenteric vasculature and bowel viability.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is WRONG?

An elevated lactate supports mesenteric ischemia

questions.correctAnswerText: Bowel strangulation/ischemia causes metabolic alkalosis and hypokalemia
questions.explanation: Bowel strangulation classically produces lactic (metabolic) acidosis from tissue hypoperfusion, not alkalosis; hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis is instead associated with vomiting/GI fluid losses, an independent mechanism.

questions.text: How do patients classically describe the pain of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm?

The most severe/worst pain of their life — sudden, severe, tearing abdominal/flank/back pain
Mild colicky pain relieved by antacids

questions.correctAnswerText: The most severe/worst pain of their life — sudden, severe, tearing abdominal/flank/back pain
questions.explanation: Ruptured AAA classically presents with sudden, excruciating, tearing pain often associated with hypotension and a pulsatile abdominal mass, reflecting acute hemorrhage into the retroperitoneum or peritoneal cavity.

questions.text: Which is the most important predictor of abdominal aortic aneurysm rupture?
questions.correctAnswer: D) Size (maximum diameter) of the aneurysm
questions.explanation: Aneurysm diameter is the single strongest predictor of rupture risk, with rapid expansion and symptomatic aneurysms also raising concern; smoking and uncontrolled hypertension are contributory but secondary risk factors.

allQuestions.text: What is the primary treatment goal in managing sinus tachycardia?

allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Identify and treat the underlying cause

allQuestions.explanation: CPR must resume immediately after a shock without pausing to check pulse or rhythm, since even a successful shock rarely produces an immediately palpable pulse; rhythm is reassessed after the 2-minute CPR cycle.

allQuestions.text: In adult cardiac arrest, when is the first dose of epinephrine given, and how often is it repeated?

1 mg IV/IO every 10 minutes throughout the arrest

allQuestions.text: Which drug is used specifically to treat torsades de pointes during cardiac arrest management?

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is used for cardiac reperfusion in an ACS patient when timely PCI is unavailable?

allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Fibrinolytic therapy, if the patient has an eligible STEMI and PCI is not available in time

allQuestions.text: In the VF/pulseless VT algorithm, when are epinephrine and amiodarone typically administered relative to defibrillation?

Epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, given during the CPR cycle after the second shock; amiodarone (or lidocaine) for refractory VF/pVT typically after the third shock
Epinephrine only once at the start; amiodarone continuously infused

allQuestions.text: A 55-year-old male has stroke symptoms, and CT shows multilobar infarction (more than one-third of the cerebral hemisphere). What therapy is contraindicated?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Thrombolytic therapy
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Thrombolytic therapy
allQuestions.explanation: A large established infarct substantially increases the risk of hemorrhagic transformation with thrombolysis; current decisions also weigh time window, disabling deficit, and modern imaging criteria rather than this legacy size cutoff alone.

allQuestions.text: A 79-year-old patient in supraventricular tachycardia has a blood pressure of 80/50 and complains of chest discomfort with near-syncope. What is the next appropriate step?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Synchronized cardioversion
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Synchronized cardioversion
allQuestions.explanation: Hypotension and chest discomfort attributable to the tachyarrhythmia define instability, requiring immediate synchronized cardioversion; carotid massage risks complications in elderly patients, and amiodarone/lidocaine are not first-line for unstable SVT.

allQuestions.text: _______ access is preferred in cardiac arrest due to easy access and no interruption in CPR.
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Peripheral
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Peripheral
allQuestions.explanation: Peripheral IV access can be obtained without interrupting chest compressions and carries fewer complications than central lines, making it the preferred first-line route during arrest.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are bradycardic rhythms except:
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Atrial fibrillation
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Atrial fibrillation
allQuestions.explanation: Atrial fibrillation is typically associated with an irregular, often rapid ventricular response, not bradycardia, unlike the listed AV blocks which characteristically slow ventricular rate.

allQuestions.text: Choose the correct sequence of electrical activity in the heart for normal sinus rhythm.

allQuestions.correctAnswerText: SA node, AV node, Bundle of His, Purkinje fibers
allQuestions.explanation: The normal conduction pathway originates in the SA node, passes through the AV node, then the Bundle of His, and finally the Purkinje fibers to depolarize the ventricles.

allQuestions.text: In children and infants, when should 2 minutes of CPR be given before activating EMS in a single-rescuer scenario?

allQuestions.text: In CPR, what is the maximum time a rescuer should take to check for a pulse?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) No more than 10 seconds

allQuestions.explanation: If a definite pulse is not felt within 10 seconds, the rescuer should begin or resume CPR without further delay to avoid prolonging a no-flow state.

allQuestions.text: Most cases of pediatric cardiac arrest begin with which underlying process?

allQuestions.text: A patient with chronic alcohol-related liver disease presents with hematemesis. Which source of upper-GI bleeding must be urgently considered?
